Adverbial Clauses of Comparison: Degree and Manner
When you compare objects or people to other objects or people, you can use adverbial clauses of comparison. </br> These make your writing and speaking sound more sophisticated and dynamic.

There are two kinds of adverbial clauses of comparison:

    1. of degree
Adverbial clauses of comparison of degree are introduced by the subordinating conjunction than, or by the relative adverb as.

For example:
She is taller than her sister. He is as rich as he is intelligent.

    2. of manner
Adverbial clauses of comparison of manner are introduced by the relative adverb as.

For example:

You may do as you like.
It is as I expected.
Apple is  as exciting as it gets for some and as difficult as it gets for others.
Manhattan was soon thought by many as the place where money changes hands as fast as the speed of light.
As early as 1860 New York was considered a financial capital - a younger rival to London itself!
The New York Stock Exchange and Wall Street has granted these downtown streets more fame than most.
Central Park was bigger than most parks dared to be.
Passives: The Simple Past and Present Perfect
You use the passive form of the Simple Past and Present Perfect tenses when the action is not done by the subject but rather to the subject. Often, it is not known who has done the action.

In articles, stories and academic writing, you often use the passive voice. This gives your writing a more sophisticated and dynamic quality.

images.text: For many years New York City has been considered by some to be the greatest city on earth, and has been thought by others to be a giant madhouse. Living in the turmoil that is the Big Apple is  as exciting as it gets for some and as difficult as it gets for others. It  is certainly perceived to have more of something for anyone who cares to dip their toes into the swirling sea of cabs and people that drift to it.</br>If you have been sent to New York on business or have been drawn to it for the shopping, art, or Broadway, take to the streets and make up your own mind.

As early as 1860 New York was considered a financial capital - a younger rival to London itself! Manhattan was soon thought by many as the place where money changes hands as fast as the speed of light. The New York Stock Exchange and Wall Street has granted these downtown streets more fame than most.</br>Thousands of fortunes have been made and have been lost on these streets. It was once said that they were paved with gold. That gold may be the gold of the unlucky whose wealth was lost, sometimes overnight.

Although the skyline has always been defined by New York's skyscrapers, many people have come to prefer the quiet spots in the city. Uptown, where Central Park, bigger than most parks dared to be,  was carved out in the late 1880s, people come to canter, ride the carousel or just find quiet. The rumble of traffic and the cacophony from the streets have been deadened. It's as great a haven as you will find anywhere.</br>Whether you love it or hate it, Manhattan remains more intriguing than most other cities anywhere.

contents.value: The Inca Empire flourished in the center of Peru  between 1438 and 1533. The Inca used peaceful means to acquire land and followers. By doing this they were able to control a significant part of South America. However, shortly after the Inca Civil War, the last emperor was killed by Francisco Pizarro. This led to the Spanish conquest of Peru in 1572.
